subsection: 6. Case study: the secession of Katanga, 1960–1965

notes.h: Background: Katanga's mineral wealth and its politics before 1960
notes.b: Katanga was the richest mining region of the Belgian Congo, and its mining economy was controlled by a Belgian company.
points: Katanga, later called Shaba, was the copper-mining heart of the Congo, and it also produced cobalt, zinc, and uranium that was used in the first atomic bombs.
The Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, a company with Belgian shareholders, ran the mines and gave Katanga a far higher revenue base than other provinces.
Katanga's administration and its mining towns, such as Élisabethville (now Lubumbashi), were dominated by Europeans, and Congolese workers lived in segregated housing.
The Conakat party, founded in 1958 by Moïse Tshombe, represented the Lunda and related peoples and campaigned for regional autonomy, arguing that Katanga should keep its own revenue.
The rival Balubakat party drew support from Baluba migrants in the mining towns, and the rivalry between the two parties became a regional and ethnic conflict.
Belgian mining interests and officials supported Conakat's autonomy campaign, which made Katanga's secession more likely once independence came.

notes.h: The secession and Belgian backing, July 1960
points: Tshombe proclaimed the secession of Katanga from the Congo on 11 July 1960, just eleven days after independence, and declared the Katangan State.
The secession was supported by Belgian officers, advisers and paid foreign mercenaries, who trained and led the Katanga Gendarmerie.
Lumumba's government saw the secession as a threat to national unity, and it asked the United Nations for help in restoring the Congo's territory.
Tshombe argued that Katanga was a separate state with its own revenue and that a central government in Léopoldville was controlled by outsiders and Communists.
The Katanga secession was not recognised by any state, and the Belgian government first denied support and later admitted its military role.

notes.h: The UN operation and the Irish troops, 1960–1961
points: The UN Security Council set up the ONUC operation in July 1960, and the UN declared that it would not intervene in internal disputes except to prevent civil war.
The UN forces were initially reluctant to challenge the Katangan state, and the Katanga secession became a test of UN powers in internal conflicts.
Irish troops, forming part of the UN force, suffered casualties in an ambush at Niemba in November 1960 and were involved in the fighting at Jadotville in September 1961.
At Jadotville, a company of Irish soldiers was besieged by Katangan gendarmes and foreign mercenaries from 13 September 1961 and surrendered after several days without relief.

Conor Cruise O'Brien, an Irish diplomat serving as the UN representative in Katanga, pressed for a more forceful UN policy, and the UN launched Operation Morthor on 24 September 1961 against Katangan roadblocks and positions.

notes.h: The death of Hammarskjöld and the end of secession, 1961–1963
points: Dag Hammarskjöld, the UN Secretary-General, died in an air crash near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia on 18 September 1961 while travelling to negotiate a ceasefire with Tshombe.
The death of Hammarskjöld was investigated by several inquiries, and the cause of the crash remains a matter of dispute among historians.
The UN's operations in Katanga were continued under U Thant, and in December 1962 the UN launched Operation Grand Slam against the Katangan forces.
Tshombe accepted a settlement in January 1963, and the Katanga secession ended on 14 January 1963, when the province was reintegrated into the Congo.
The secession had lasted about two and a half years, and its end removed the largest threat to the central government's authority.

notes.h: Tshombe, Mobutu and the Congo's new order, 1963–1965
points: Tshombe became prime minister of the Congo in July 1964, a post he held until his dismissal by President Kasa-Vubu in October 1965.
The Simba rebellion of 1964, by supporters of Lumumba, spread through the east of the Congo and was defeated with Belgian and American help in 1964–65.
Mobutu, who had been army chief of staff since 1960, seized power on 24 November 1965, and Tshombe went into exile in Spain.
The Katanga secession had shown the army's importance and the effect of foreign support, and Mobutu's coup used the army to end the factional fighting of the 1960s.

In 1977 and 1978 the Shaba invasions by Katangan exiles from Angola were defeated with the help of Moroccan forces and Belgian and French paratroops, showing that Katanga remained a source of instability.

notes.b: Mobutu rose from the army to become the dictator of the Congo, which he renamed Zaire, and ruled it until 1997.
points: Born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala in the Congo, he served in the Force Publique and rose to the rank of sergeant-major before independence.
He became chief of staff of the Congolese army in 1960, and in September 1960 he took power and suspended the government and parliament for two years.
As a participant in the Katanga crisis he supported the central government against the secession, while his army was supplied and trained with American and Belgian assistance.
He seized power a second time on 24 November 1965, and he ruled as president under a one-party system from 1967 onwards.
Contemporaries in the West, including the United States and Belgium, regarded him as a bulwark against communism in central Africa; many Congolese saw him as a corrupt ruler who enriched his circle.
Historians see his rule as a case of personal dictatorship and clientelism, which left the state weak, and they debate the extent of Western support for his regime.
He changed the country's name to Zaire in 1971 and his own name to Mobutu Sese Seko in 1972; he was overthrown by Laurent-Désiré Kabila's forces in 1997 and died in exile that September.
Nationally, the secession tested whether the Congo could survive as one state, and the central government's victory preserved its territory.
Internationally, the crisis was a Cold War contest in which the United States and the Soviet Union, and the former colonial power Belgium, each supported different sides.
The Katanga case set a precedent for the UN's involvement in internal conflicts and for its peacekeeping role, which became a standard tool of the organisation.
The Katanga case also showed the continuing power of foreign mining companies in African politics, and Union Minière's wealth continued after independence.
The crisis weakened the reputation of the UN in some states because the Security Council's authorisation came after months of argument over its mandate.

notes.h: Assessment: why Katanga seceded and why it drew international involvement
points: Cause: Katanga's mineral revenues gave its leaders a strong economic reason to keep control of their wealth, and Belgian companies and officials supported that aim.
Cause: Tshombe's Conakat party claimed that Katanga's peoples had a separate identity, and the fear of Lumumba's centralising government strengthened regional loyalties.
Result: the secession was defeated by the central government with UN help, but the crisis left the Congolese state dependent on foreign military support.
International involvement came from Belgian self-interest, Cold War rivalry and the UN's need to protect a new member state's territorial integrity.
Contemporary view: the Congolese government and many African states saw the secession as a neo-colonial plot, while Tshombe and his supporters saw it as a defence against centralised rule.
Later view: historians generally see Katanga as the clearest case of how economic interests and foreign backing could sustain a secession, and they stress the role of Belgium and the mining company.

keyTerms.definition: A term used by colonial officials for loyalty to ethnic groups, which in Katanga shaped the rivalry between the Conakat and Balubakat parties.
An economy in which companies and capital operate across national borders, as with the Union Minière's control of Katangan mining.
The withdrawal of a region from a state to form a separate state, as Katanga did from July 1960 to January 1963.
The Belgian-controlled mining company that ran Katanga's copper, cobalt and uranium industries.
A foreign soldier paid to fight for a state or faction, who served in the Katanga Gendarmerie and against the UN forces.
The rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from 1945 to 1991, which shaped the Katanga crisis and the Congo's politics.
Mobutu's policy from 1971 to promote African culture and names, and to reject European influence.
The deployment of UN forces to keep order and separate combatants, as in ONUC in the Congo from 1960.
